fileDoc.summary: Exact base-ten arithmetic.
fileDoc.description: `Half`, `Float`, `Double` and `Quad` are binary floating point: they store a significand times a power of *two*, so `0.1` is not a value any of them has, however many bits they are given. A price is base ten, and so is every rule about how a price rounds, which is why money belongs here and not there. A [Decimal] is `coefficient × 10^-scale` - an integer and how far to move its point. `19.99` is `1999` at scale `2`, exactly, and stays exact through every addition. It is built out of a `Cent`, so this is a library type: no backend has a base-ten number, and none is asked for one. Two values that are numerically equal need not be identical: `1.5` is scale `1` and `1.50` is scale `2`. [compareTo] and `==` compare the numbers; [trimmed] is how a value drops the zeroes it does not need.

fileDoc.summary: Stream builders and the types they produce.
fileDoc.description: A `Sequence<T>` is a synchronous series of values; a `Flow<T>` is the asynchronous counterpart. Both are ordinary library types rather than language constructs, so a producer stays an ordinary `func` and only its return type says what kind of stream it is: ```azora func values(): Sequence<Int> = sequence<Int> [!] s: SequenceScope<Int> { yield(1) yield(2) } func countdown(from: Int): Flow<Int> = flow<Int> [!] c: FlowCollector<Int> { for n in from..0 { emit(n) } } ``` The builder runs its producer to completion when it is called, collecting every value into the stream. Consumers therefore never observe a partially produced stream, and a producer that never finishes never returns - an unbounded `while true { yield … }` does not terminate.

fileDoc.summary: Proposed native map hierarchy for Azora.
fileDoc.description: Maps use operators supplied by their key and value types. There are no runtime hasher, equality, or comparator objects: - `HashMap<K, V>` and `LinkedHashMap<K, V>` require `Hash` and `oper==` for `K`. - `TreeMap<K, V>` requires `oper<` for `K`. - `containsValue`, structural `oper==`, and structural `Hash` instantiate only when the corresponding value operators exist. `oper[start:stop:step]` returns a snapshot of the map's entries using its iteration order. `start` is inclusive, `stop` is exclusive, and `step` defaults to `1`. fileDoc.summary: Rendering-independent reactive state, derived values, and deterministic
fileDoc.description: `react func` and `react async func` create reactive owners. A state lifetime is combined with an ordinary binding form: - `remember var count = 0` survives reruns of its owner. - `retain fin model = loadModel()` survives owner recreation in-process. - `preserve val draft = Draft()` can be snapshotted and restored. `lazy fin` is a one-shot lazy binding outside a reactive owner. Inside a reactive owner it is also a cached derived value: reactive reads invalidate it and its next read recomputes it. Effects are synchronous and deterministic: - `effect { ... }` tracks reactive values actually read by the body. - `effect value { ... }` observes one explicit dependency. - `effect [a, b] { ... }` observes an explicit dependency list. - `effect defer { ... }` runs when its owner is disposed.

fileDoc.summary: Deterministic, format-independent serialization primitives.
fileDoc.description: A `Serializer<T>` converts a typed value to and from `SerialValue`. The text format is a separate concern: `encodeSerialValue` and `decodeSerialValue` handle canonical AZON, the one format the standard library ships. This separation lets an application reuse one typed serializer with a wire format of its own, and makes custom serializers straightforward for values owned by another library. AZON is the only built-in format. Any other - JSON, CBOR, YAML, a private wire format - is written outside the standard library by implementing `Serializer<T>` and encoding the resulting `SerialValue`. Numbers are retained as validated source text instead of being converted to `Double`; this prevents precision loss for large integers and decimal values. Object fields preserve insertion order. Duplicate fields are rejected while decoding unless explicitly enabled in `SerializerOptions`. This API is experimental, but its wire-format rules are intentionally strict so data written today can remain readable as the implementation evolves.
